questions.question: Did aspirin reduce the risk of cardiovascular events in the primary prevention trials ARRIVE, ASCEND, ASPREE and JPPP? Give each trial's result.

keyPoints.text: ARRIVE (moderate-risk patients): no significant difference in the primary endpoint (4.29% vs 4.48%, hazard ratio 0.96; 95% CI 0.81 to 1.13).

support.quote: the primary endpoint occurred in 269 (4·29%) patients in the aspirin group versus 281 (4·48%) patients in the placebo group (hazard ratio [HR] 0·96; 95% CI 0·81-1·13; p=0·6038)

keyPoints.text: ASCEND (diabetes): serious vascular events were significantly lower with aspirin (8.5% vs 9.6%, rate ratio 0.88; 95% CI 0.79 to 0.97).

support.quote: serious vascular events occurred in a significantly lower percentage of participants in the aspirin group than in the placebo group (658 participants [8.5%] vs. 743 [9.6%]; rate ratio, 0.88; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.79 to 0.97; P=0.01)

keyPoints.text: ASPREE (healthy older adults): cardiovascular disease was not significantly lower with aspirin (10.7 vs 11.3 events per 1000 person-years, hazard ratio 0.95; 95% CI 0.83 to 1.08).

support.quote: the rate of cardiovascular disease was 10.7 events per 1000 person-years in the aspirin group and 11.3 events per 1000 person-years in the placebo group (hazard ratio, 0.95; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.83 to 1.08)

keyPoints.text: JPPP (Japanese patients aged 60 to 85 with risk factors): the 5-year primary outcome rate was not significantly different (2.77% vs 2.96%, hazard ratio 0.94; 95% CI 0.77 to 1.15).

support.quote: The 5-year cumulative primary outcome event rate was not significantly different between the groups (2.77% [95% CI, 2.40%-3.20%] for aspirin vs 2.96% [95% CI, 2.58%-3.40%] for no aspirin; hazard ratio [HR], 0.94 [95% CI, 0.77-1.15]; P = .54)

questions.question: What do the trials and meta-analyses show about the bleeding risk of aspirin in primary prevention? Give the figures from ASCEND, ASPREE, ARRIVE, the 2019 JAMA meta-analysis and the 2009 collaborative meta-analysis.

keyPoints.text: ASCEND: major bleeding occurred in 4.1% with aspirin versus 3.2% with placebo (rate ratio 1.29; 95% CI 1.09 to 1.52), mostly gastrointestinal and other extracranial bleeding.

support.quote: major bleeding events occurred in 314 participants (4.1%) in the aspirin group, as compared with 245 (3.2%) in the placebo group (rate ratio, 1.29; 95% CI, 1.09 to 1.52; P=0.003), with most of the excess being gastrointestinal bleeding and other extracranial bleeding

keyPoints.text: ASPREE: major hemorrhage was 8.6 versus 6.2 events per 1000 person-years (hazard ratio 1.38; 95% CI 1.18 to 1.62).

support.quote: The rate of major hemorrhage was 8.6 events per 1000 person-years and 6.2 events per 1000 person-years, respectively (hazard ratio, 1.38; 95% CI, 1.18 to 1.62; P<0.001)

keyPoints.text: ARRIVE: gastrointestinal bleeding events (mostly mild) were 0.97% with aspirin versus 0.46% with placebo (hazard ratio 2.11; 95% CI 1.36 to 3.28).

support.quote: Gastrointestinal bleeding events (mostly mild) occurred in 61 (0·97%) patients in the aspirin group versus 29 (0·46%) in the placebo group (HR 2·11; 95% CI 1·36-3·28; p=0·0007)

keyPoints.text: The 2019 JAMA meta-analysis found major bleeding increased with aspirin (hazard ratio 1.43; absolute risk increase 0.47%; number needed to harm 210).

support.quote: (HR, 1.43 [95% credible interval, 1.30-1.56]; absolute risk increase, 0.47% [95% CI, 0.34%-0.62%]; number needed to harm, 210)

keyPoints.text: The 2009 collaborative meta-analysis found aspirin allocation increased major gastrointestinal and extracranial bleeds (0.10% vs 0.07% per year).

support.quote: Aspirin allocation increased major gastrointestinal and extracranial bleeds (0.10%vs 0.07% per year, p<0.0001)

questions.question: How do the 2009 collaborative meta-analysis and the 2019 JAMA meta-analysis compare in the size of the cardiovascular benefit and the bleeding harm of aspirin in primary prevention, and how did each frame the net balance?

keyPoints.text: The 2009 collaborative meta-analysis found a 12% proportional reduction in serious vascular events in primary prevention (0.51% vs 0.57% per year).

support.quote: aspirin allocation yielded a 12% proportional reduction in serious vascular events (0.51% aspirin vs 0.57% control per year, p=0.0001)

keyPoints.text: The 2009 authors judged aspirin in primary prevention to be of uncertain net value, because the reduction in occlusive events has to be weighed against an increase in major bleeds.

support.quote: In primary prevention without previous disease, aspirin is of uncertain net value as the reduction in occlusive events needs to be weighed against any increase in major bleeds.

keyPoints.text: The 2019 JAMA meta-analysis (13 trials) found a lower risk of the composite cardiovascular outcome (hazard ratio 0.89; absolute risk reduction 0.38%; number needed to treat 265).

support.quote: 0.89 [95% credible interval, 0.84-0.95]; absolute risk reduction, 0.38% [95% CI, 0.20%-0.55%]; number needed to treat, 265)

keyPoints.text: The 2019 meta-analysis found major bleeding up (hazard ratio 1.43; absolute risk increase 0.47%; number needed to harm 210) and concluded that aspirin was associated with a lower risk of cardiovascular events and an increased risk of major bleeding.

support.quote: The use of aspirin in individuals without cardiovascular disease was associated with a lower risk of cardiovascular events and an increased risk of major bleeding.
number needed to harm, 210

questions.question: What did ASPREE report about all-cause mortality and cancer deaths with aspirin, and how does that compare with the mortality and cancer findings of ARRIVE and ASCEND?

keyPoints.text: ASPREE: all-cause mortality was higher with aspirin (12.7 vs 11.1 events per 1000 person-years, hazard ratio 1.14; 95% CI 1.01 to 1.29).

support.quote: The risk of death from any cause was 12.7 events per 1000 person-years in the aspirin group and 11.1 events per 1000 person-years in the placebo group (hazard ratio, 1.14; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.01 to 1.29)

keyPoints.text: In ASPREE cancer was the major contributor: cancer-related death occurred in 3.1% with aspirin and 2.3% with placebo (hazard ratio 1.31); the authors called the result unexpected and to be interpreted with caution.

support.quote: Cancer-related death occurred in 3.1% of the participants in the aspirin group and in 2.3% of those in the placebo group (hazard ratio, 1.31; 95% CI, 1.10 to 1.56)
this result was unexpected and should be interpreted with caution

keyPoints.text: ASCEND found no significant difference in gastrointestinal tract cancer (2.0% vs 2.0%) or all cancers (11.6% vs 11.5%).

support.quote: no significant difference between the aspirin group and the placebo group in the incidence of gastrointestinal tract cancer (157 participants [2.0%] and 158 [2.0%], respectively) or all cancers (897 [11.6%] and 887 [11.5%])

keyPoints.text: ARRIVE found documented deaths to be similar in the two groups (2.55% with aspirin vs 2.57% with placebo).

support.quote: There were 321 documented deaths in the intention-to-treat population (n=160 [2·55%] vs n=161 [2·57%] of 6276 patients in the placebo group)

questions.question: Which populations did ARRIVE, ASPREE and JPPP enroll, and how do the US Preventive Services Task Force recommendations for adults aged 40 to 59 and 60 or older relate to that evidence?

keyPoints.text: ARRIVE enrolled patients aged 55 (men) or 60 (women) or older at moderate cardiovascular risk and excluded patients at high bleeding risk or with diabetes.

support.quote: Eligible patients were aged 55 years (men) or 60 years (women) and older and had an average cardiovascular risk, deemed to be moderate on the basis of the number of specific risk factors. We excluded patients at high risk of gastrointestinal bleeding or other bleeding, or diabetes.

keyPoints.text: ASPREE enrolled community-dwelling adults aged 70 or older (65 or older among Black and Hispanic persons in the US) without cardiovascular disease, dementia or disability.

support.quote: who were 70 years of age or older (or ≥65 years of age among blacks and Hispanics in the United States) and did not have cardiovascular disease, dementia, or disability

keyPoints.text: JPPP enrolled Japanese patients aged 60 to 85 with hypertension, dyslipidemia or diabetes mellitus.

support.quote: Patients (N = 14,464) were aged 60 to 85 years, presenting with hypertension, dyslipidemia, or diabetes mellitus

keyPoints.text: The USPSTF makes initiating low-dose aspirin an individual decision for adults aged 40 to 59 with a 10% or greater 10-year cardiovascular risk (small net benefit, C recommendation) and recommends against initiating it in adults 60 or older (D recommendation).

support.quote: The decision to initiate low-dose aspirin use for the primary prevention of CVD in adults aged 40 to 59 years who have a 10% or greater 10-year CVD risk should be an individual one.
The USPSTF recommends against initiating low-dose aspirin use for the primary prevention of CVD in adults 60 years or older. (D recommendation).

questions.question: How many participants were randomized in ASCEND, and what aspirin dose did they receive?

keyPoints.text: 15,480 participants underwent randomization.

support.quote: A total of 15,480 participants underwent randomization.

keyPoints.text: Aspirin was given at 100 mg daily (against matching placebo).

questions.question: In JPPP, what were the 5-year cumulative primary outcome event rates with aspirin and without aspirin, and the hazard ratio?

keyPoints.text: The 5-year cumulative primary outcome event rate was 2.77% with aspirin and 2.96% without aspirin.
The hazard ratio was 0.94 (95% CI 0.77 to 1.15; P = .54).

questions.question: Why was JPPP terminated early, and after what median follow-up?

keyPoints.text: The data monitoring committee terminated it early based on likely futility.

support.quote: The study was terminated early by the data monitoring committee after a median follow-up of 5.02 years (interquartile range, 4.55-5.33) based on likely futility.

keyPoints.text: The median follow-up at termination was 5.02 years.

support.quote: after a median follow-up of 5.02 years
